title: Differentiable Systematic Resampling for Variational Sequential Monte Carlo
claim: Hard resampling gives a sharp banded assignment; our relaxation keeps that ordered band structure while smoothing it, unlike a diffuse optimal-transport alternative.
layout: 3 heatmap panels side by side, shared colorbar, left-to-right comparison
description: Three square heatmaps sit in a row and show transportation matrices T_ji. The x-axis is ancestor particle i and the y-axis is resampled particle j, with 25 particles. A shared viridis colorbar from 0 to 1 is on the right. The left panel, Hard SR, shows bright yellow single-cell blocks that run diagonally from top-left to bottom-right, a staircase on a dark purple background. This is the exact systematic resampling map. The middle panel, DSR with τ=0.1, shows a smooth, soft diagonal band in teal and blue that follows the same staircase and spreads it slightly. The right panel, EROT with ε=0.5, shows diffuse, scattered, noisy purple and blue cells with no clear banded structure and a few brighter blotches. The eye goes first to the yellow staircase, then compares the other two panels against it.
caption: Transportation maps for systematic resampling (left), DSR (middle), and EROT (right), for a sequential importance resampling PF of the Lorenz-63 system. The transportation maps are calculated at step $150$ using $N=25$ particles, and DSR and EROT use the training relaxation parameters.
abstract: Particle filters are a standard tool for nonlinear state estimation, but their resampling step is discrete, preventing gradient-based learning in variational sequential Monte Carlo. We introduce Differentiable Systematic Resampling (DSR), a temperature-controlled relaxation of systematic resampling, that preserves the CDF-ordered, banded structure of systematic resampling while enabling full gradient flow. DSR converges to exact systematic resampling as the temperature vanishes, and we prove a pointwise exponential convergence rate for the induced bias. Compared to optimal-transport-based differentiable resampling, DSR avoids iterative solvers and has substantially lower computational overhead. Experiments on stochastic dynamical systems and real-world handwriting data show that DSR achieves comparable or superior filtering and dynamics learning performance.
